name: Network client hints (ECT, RTT, Downlink)
plain: Server-side headers with the effective connection type, RTT and downlink.
meaning: Same numbers as the Network Information API but delivered on requests so the server can adapt before sending HTML. Requires Accept-CH opt-in, with the same 25 ms and 25 kbps rounding.

web.api: Accept-CH: ECT, RTT, Downlink; request headers ECT, RTT, Downlink

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

limits.headline: Can see your rough connection speed and delay in each request, if it asks first
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens after the site opts in, on each page load
can: Receive speed and delay hints with your request
Send a lighter page if your connection is slow
Notice when your connection class changes between visits
cannot: Get exact speed, since figures are rounded to coarse steps
Get anything unless the site opts in first
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge and Samsung Internet send it. Firefox and Safari do not.

story.what_it_is: Servers can receive a note about your connection type, delay and speed with each request.

marketing.name: ECT header
marketing.pitch: Tells the server the browser's effective connection type, so it can pick lighter or richer content.

story.for_you: You never see it. If a site asks, your browser tells its server how good the connection seems. The server may send a smaller page if the line is slow.
story.for_makers: Makers can decide what to send before the browser runs any script. That saves time for slow users. The details also add a small clue to a device fingerprint.

use_cases.example: A video platform reads the hint on the first request and picks a lower starting quality for slow connections.
A store sends a short list of products with small pictures on slow lines, and the full page on fast ones.
A news site serves a text first version on slow connections, and loads pictures later.
A browser game site serves a smaller loader and delays heavy assets for players on slow lines.
An ad server picks a lightweight ad for slow connections so the page is not blocked.
A speed monitoring tool groups real page load times by connection type from the headers.
A government site gives a plain, light page to people on slow rural internet, so forms still work.
